description:
There is always a misconception of what makes a super premium chocolate ice cream, people always think it should be physical chocolate only and that cocoa powder is "cheap". That is so incorrect and hopefully you are learning as we go through this chocolate ice cream journey, that the luxury chocolate ice creams out there are most likely cocoa powder or combinations of the two. 

Todays video is an introduction in to ice cream calculators and how a base (unbalanced) recipe differers when using both options. 

The 56% chocolate version, you can obviously add more chocolate but you start to increase the solids each time which can become a problem. 

Later in the series we will show you how to create an amazing chocolate ice cream using only real chocolate but for now, lets compare. 

The recipes we use here are:

Cocoa powder base (unbalanced):
500g whole milk
400g double cream @ 49% fat
220g sugar
54g SMP
50g Cocoa powder @21% fat
17.9% fat, 9.3% MSNF, 18% sugar, 48% solids.


Chocolate base (unbalanced): 
480g milk
300g double cream @ 49% fat
90g sugar
75g chocolate at 55-56% cocoa solids
40g SMP
18.8% fat, 9.6% MSNF, 17.8% sugar, 42.5% solids

comments.text:
Hi Nick, thanks for the great content as always. Is it correct that the % referenced on a cocoa powder tells us the fat % but the % listed on a chocolate, like the Barima 56% here, tells us how much of it is cocoa (mass and butter)? Not nitpicking but you said the Barima has 56% fat, so I'm just checking my understanding!

Also, I know you were explicit here in not going for a really balanced recipe but isnt 18-19% fat quite high? Thanks~
comments.author: @troy82926

comments.text: You are correct in that cocoa powder is fat%, chocolate is cocoa solids%. I don’t know why I said fat for chocolate all those years ago. 18-19% is high in North American because cream is awful and goes greasy above about 14%. UK(where this video was made), 18% is fine as it’s much better quality. It’s still high but there are some luxury EU ice creams sold at 24% fat!
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery

comments.text: @PolarIceCreamery interesting so the absolute fat content isn’t necessarily responsible for that greasiness at high levels but rather the quality of the source of the fat. Thanks for the response!

comments.text: @troy82926  to a degree yes that is the case. Poor quality fat (such as most available in the store here) don’t allow anything over 15% without going greasy. UK double cream, UK clotted cream, mascarpone etc will allow a much higher fat content.

comments.text:
POD is a personal preference really. People like sweet food predominantly, there will always be people who prefer less sweet foods. The problem is the people who argue until they’re blue in the face about ice cream being too sweet…. Also want it easily scoopable. White it can be achieved to a degree, the resulting recipes are difficult to get right and most people just want to make ice cream and eat it without the fuss. 
I will do a video about soon but serving temps is the point that scoop/eat it. Most homes freezers are too cold to serve straight from the freezer but again, that can be resolved with adjustments to sugar types and amounts. 
Fructose, dextrose, sucrose, invert, liquid glucose, inulin, xylitol etc etc all the sugar and sugar alcohols have different relative sweetness levels and they also have different solids contents.

comments.author: @s.y.4150

comments.text:
I order my ingredients from various places and spend way to much time and money on experimenting haha. I normally use Henley Bridge and Vantage House for most things, they are both UK based suppliers. 
The heating of everything or leave the cream until the end is recipe specific to be honest. Cocoa Powder bases (along with some other bases) can take the cream after, it helps to cool the base down quickly. If you use real chocolate, you need to watch the cocoa solids coming back together as they will not be emulsified within the cream if you add it after. There are also the proteins in the cream which some say absolutely need to be denatured and adding the cream after stops this happening ( I disagree that it NEEDS to be done). So there is a lot to consider and as mentioned, most recipes are different and need to be thought of individually. 
Finally, you need to find a method that suits YOU. We do things differently and if eveyone did it the same, all ice cream would be identical.
comments.author: @PolarIceCreamery
